title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: Sharing parameters across recurrences gives less capacity than unique layers, and a fitted partial-equivalence law matches observed compute-optimal losses where the standard form does not.
layout: 2 plots side-by-side; left ratio curves with shaded gap, right loss-vs-compute fits
description: Two line plots sit side by side. The left plot has recurrence count r (1, 2, 4, 8) on the x-axis and the ratio versus r=1 on the y-axis. A flat green line shows forward FLOPs staying constant. A dashed purple line with squares shows unique parameters falling to 0.31×. A bold blue line with diamonds shows effective shared capacity falling more slowly, to 0.47×. The gray shaded area between the green and blue lines is labeled parameter-sharing cost, and each point has a numeric annotation. The right plot shows compute-optimal validation loss against training compute on a log x-axis, with four colored curves for r=1, 2, 4 and 8. Crosses mark empirical optima that sit on the solid fitted curves. A thick dashed gray curve for the standard φ=1 form passes through the middle of the bundle and misses every curve. Legends are above both plots.
caption: Left: at matched effective depth, per-token forward FLOPs $F(r)$ stay flat while unique parameters $N(r)$ drop as $r$ grows. Shared parameter capacity $N_once + r^{\varphi} N_rec$ with $\varphi{=}0.46$ drops more slowly. Right: compute-optimal validation loss per architecture against compute budget $C$. Empirical per-budget optima (crosses) track our $\varphi{=}0.46$ fit (solid curves). The standard form ($\varphi{=}1$) collapses all four architectures onto a single curve (dashed), which fits none of the empirical results.
abstract: We measure how much one recurrence is worth to a looped transformer in equivalent unique parameters. From an iso-depth pretraining sweep across recurrence counts $r \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$ spanning ${\sim}50\times$ in training compute, we fit a joint scaling law $L = E + A\,(N_\text{once} + r^Ï N_\text{rec})^{-Î±} + B\,D^{-Î²}$ and measure a recurrence-equivalence exponent $Ï= 0.46$. Intuitively, $Ï$ tells us whether looping a block $r$ times is equivalent in validation loss to $r$ unique blocks of a non-looped model (full equivalence, $Ï{=}1$) or to a single block run repeatedly with no capacity gain ($Ï{=}0$). Our $Ï= 0.46$ sits in between, so replacing unique blocks with shared recurrences increases validation loss at matched training compute. For example, at $r{=}4$ a 410M looped model performs on par with a 580M non-looped model, but incurs the training cost of a 1B non-looped one. We demonstrate the utility of $Ï$ as a diagnostic tool on two case studies: commonly used truncated backpropagation lowers $Ï$ to $0.38$, indicating that the loop mechanism is poorly trained under truncation, even though validation loss decreases. Conversely, hyperconnections raise $Ï$ to $0.65$, a genuine capacity gain. Our method separates true loop improvements from training-side gains, a distinction raw validation loss cannot make. Code is available at https://github.com/kschwethelm/looped-lm-scaling.
